lead: Electrical discharge machining removes metal with sparks, not a cutting edge. A shaped tool electrode and the workpiece sit in a tank of dielectric fluid, a few tens of micrometres apart, and a pulse generator drives thousands of sparks per second across the gap. Each spark melts and flings away a crater of metal. The tool never touches the work, so there is no cutting force and very hard or very thin parts can be cut. Dies, moulds, press tools and hard alloys are the everyday work.
prereq: You need: 6.2 for servo feed drives, and the basic electrical ideas of voltage, current and energy.

blocks.text: EDM uses a shaped tool electrode and the workpiece, both dipped in dielectric fluid — kerosene for most die work, deionised water in wire machines. The tool is the cathode, wired to the negative side of a DC pulse generator. The workpiece is the anode, on the positive side. They never touch; a gap of a few tens of micrometres stays between them.
The dielectric insulates the gap between pulses, breaks down to form the spark channel, cools the gap, and carries the eroded debris out.

items: The pulse generator raises the voltage across the gap and stresses the dielectric.
At the narrowest point the dielectric breaks down into a thin plasma channel a few micrometres wide.
Current heats the channel to several thousand degrees, so a tiny volume of tool and work melts and partly vaporises.
The pulse switches off, the channel collapses, the molten metal is thrown out, and a crater is left in the work.
Fresh dielectric sweeps the debris away and the servo head advances the electrode to restore the gap.

blocks.text: The gap sets everything. Too wide and no spark forms; too narrow and the electrode touches the work, or the spark becomes a continuous arc that burns the surface. Removal rate changes as the cavity deepens, so a fixed down-feed loses the gap. The servo head measures the average gap voltage, which rises as the gap widens, compares it with a set value, and moves the electrode to hold the gap. This is the closed-loop position control used on CNC feed drives (see 6.2).

One spark is described by its on-time, off-time, peak current and gap voltage. On-time ton is how long the pulse lasts. Off-time toff is the pause before the next pulse. Peak current Ip is the current the channel carries. Gap voltage Vg is the voltage across the gap during the discharge.

blocks.where: E<sub>s</sub> is the energy of one spark in joules (J); V<sub>g</sub> is the gap voltage in volts (V); I<sub>p</sub> is the peak current in amperes (A); t<sub>on</sub> is the pulse on-time in seconds (s).

blocks.text: f = 1 ÷ (t<sub>on</sub> + t<sub>off</sub>),   duty cycle = t<sub>on</sub> ÷ (t<sub>on</sub> + t<sub>off</sub>),   P<sub>avg</sub> = E<sub>s</sub> × f
blocks.where: f is the pulse frequency in hertz, that is sparks per second; the duty cycle is a fraction (or a percentage); P<sub>avg</sub> is the average power delivered to the gap in watts (W).

blocks.text: A long on-time and a high peak current make a bigger, hotter spark: removal is faster, but the crater is larger, so the surface is rougher and the recast layer thicker. A short off-time leaves too little time to flush; the gap fills with conducting particles and the spark wanders into stray arcs that damage the surface.

The tool erodes as well as the work. The wear ratio is the volume of electrode lost divided by the volume of work removed. Graphite gives fast cutting at high current with low wear and is used for roughing. Copper gives a better surface at fine settings. Brass wire is the standard wire electrode; tungsten and coated wires cut fine work. Because the electrode shrinks, a deep cavity needs a roughing electrode and one or more fresh finishing electrodes to hold size.

sections.h3: Die-sinking, wire EDM and process limits

blocks.text: In die-sinking (ram EDM), the tool electrode is a mirror shape of the cavity wanted, and it is sunk into the work: forging dies, injection moulds, extrusion dies. In wire EDM, the electrode is a brass wire 0.1 to 0.3 mm thick, travelling from a spool to a take-up reel so no part of it cuts twice. The work is usually a plate cut on a two-axis path, or four axes for taper. The cut is wider than the wire by the spark gap on each side; that extra width is the overcut.

Debris left in the gap causes stray sparks, so flushing matters. Side flushing jets dielectric between electrode and cavity wall; through-flushing pushes it down a hole in the electrode; suction pulls it out through the electrode; wire machines jet fluid from above and below the plate.

The workpiece must conduct electricity. Steels, aluminium, brass, titanium, tungsten carbide and graphite are cut; plastics and ordinary ceramics are not. A hotter spark also erodes sideways, so higher current and longer on-time raise overcut as well as roughness. The recast layer is a thin resolidified skin, a few micrometres to tens of micrometres, left on the cut surface; it is hard and brittle and is often removed by a low-current finishing pass or by polishing.

Advantages: no cutting force, so thin walls and slender electrodes survive; hardness does not matter; complex cavities, sharp internal corners and fine finishes are possible. Limits: conductive work only, slow compared with milling, electrode wear, recast layer. Uses: press tools and punches, forging dies, plastic moulds, carbide parts, turbine components, micro-holes such as fuel-injector nozzles.

examples.question: An EDM run uses gap voltage 25 V, peak current 20 A, pulse on-time 100 µs and off-time 100 µs. Find the energy per spark, the pulse frequency, the duty cycle and the average power delivered to the gap.
steps: Given: V<sub>g</sub> = 25 V, I<sub>p</sub> = 20 A, t<sub>on</sub> = 100 µs = 100 × 10⁻⁶ s, t<sub>off</sub> = 100 µs = 100 × 10⁻⁶ s.
Energy per spark: E<sub>s</sub> = V<sub>g</sub> × I<sub>p</sub> × t<sub>on</sub> = 25 × 20 × 100 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.05 J.
Period of one cycle: T = t<sub>on</sub> + t<sub>off</sub> = 200 µs = 200 × 10⁻⁶ s.
Frequency: f = 1 ÷ T = 1 ÷ (200 × 10⁻⁶) = 5000 sparks per second.
Duty cycle = t<sub>on</sub> ÷ T = 100 ÷ 200 = 0.5, that is 50 %.
Average power: P<sub>avg</sub> = E<sub>s</sub> × f = 0.05 × 5000 = 250 W. Check: V<sub>g</sub> × I<sub>p</sub> × duty cycle = 25 × 20 × 0.5 = 250 W.
examples.answer: Each spark carries 0.05 J, the generator fires 5000 sparks per second, the duty cycle is 0.5 (50 %), and the average power into the gap is 250 W.
examples.check:
V_g = 25.0
I_p = 20.0
t_on = 100e-6
t_off = 100e-6
E_s = V_g * I_p * t_on
f = 1.0 / (t_on + t_off)
duty = t_on / (t_on + t_off)
P_avg = E_s * f
print(E_s)
print(f)
print(duty)
print(P_avg)

traps: Thinking EDM cuts any material. The work must conduct electricity, so plastics and ordinary ceramics cannot be cut.
Mixing up wire EDM, where a travelling wire is the electrode, with die-sinking, where a shaped electrode is sunk into the work.

Writing duty cycle as t<sub>on</sub> ÷ t<sub>off</sub>. It is t<sub>on</sub> ÷ (t<sub>on</sub> + t<sub>off</sub>), and microsecond times must be converted to seconds before computing energy in joules.
Claiming higher current improves everything. It raises removal rate but makes the surface rougher and deepens the recast layer and overcut.
Forgetting the servo. A fixed down-feed cannot hold a gap of tens of micrometres, so gap voltage feedback is the answer to 'why servo control?'.

quiz.q: Name the jobs the dielectric fluid does in EDM.
quiz.a: It insulates the gap between pulses, ionises to form the spark channel, cools the gap, and flushes the eroded debris away.

quiz.q: Why does feeding the electrode down at a fixed rate fail in EDM?
quiz.a: Removal rate changes as the cavity deepens, so the gap either closes until the electrode touches or arcs, or opens until no spark forms. The servo head must read the gap voltage and adjust the feed to hold the gap at a few tens of micrometres.

quiz.q: A spark has gap voltage 20 V, peak current 10 A, on-time 50 µs and off-time 150 µs. Find the energy per spark, the frequency, the duty cycle and the average power.
quiz.a: E<sub>s</sub> = 20 × 10 × 50 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.01 J. T = 200 µs, so f = 1 ÷ 200 × 10⁻⁶ = 5000 sparks per second. Duty cycle = 50 ÷ 200 = 0.25 (25 %). P<sub>avg</sub> = 0.01 × 5000 = 50 W, which also equals 20 × 10 × 0.25.

quiz.q: A workshop tries to EDM a glass plate and a hardened steel die with the same setting. Explain what happens in each case.
quiz.a: Glass does not conduct, so the spark cannot complete the path to the return; no erosion occurs and the machine can only arc or do nothing. Steel conducts, so each pulse melts a crater and the cavity is reproduced in the shape of the electrode, with a recast layer on the surface.

quiz.q: Why are graphite and copper used as tool electrodes, and what is the wear ratio?
quiz.a: Graphite carries high current with low electrode wear, so it roughs fast; copper holds a better surface at fine settings. The wear ratio is the volume of electrode worn divided by the volume of work removed. Wear makes the cavity undersized, so finishing electrodes are used.

quiz.q: A wire EDM uses a wire of diameter 0.25 mm and the spark overcut is 0.025 mm on each side. Find the kerf width of the cut.

beyond: Not for the exam. Micro-EDM makes holes below 100 µm. EDM milling sweeps a simple rotating rod along a path instead of sinking a shaped electrode, so one tool makes many shapes. Powder-mixed EDM adds fine powder to the dielectric for better finish; dry EDM uses a gas jet instead of a liquid. Hybrid EDM–electrochemical setups and spark monitoring for adaptive control are active research areas.
